To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic nicotine administration in male rats increased NO metabolites and neuronal NOS/NADP‐diaphoraze‐positive neurons.
chronic nicotine administration in rats increases nitric oxide metabolites in brain areas but has no effect on neuronal nitric oxide synthases.

chronic administration of nicotine increases NO production in several brain areas of both male and females rats, and this effect is not related with a significant increase in the expression or activity of NOS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of nitric oxide ( NO) in the central nervous system, particularly in the context of the neurochemical and neuropharmacological mechanisms of nicotine addiction.
the role of the endogenous opioid system in the regulation of the cardiovascular system, and the effects of chronic nicotine administration.
the effects of nicotine and nicotine‐like substances on nitric oxide production in rat brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of chronic nicotine administration depend on several parameters such as the dose, the duration, and the time of administration, and the gender of the animals.
the effects of chronic nicotine treatment on NOS activity are regionally dependent, and the cellular origin of NO synthesis is not restricted to neurons.
nicotine increases NO levels in brain regions, but this effect does not appear to be related to changes in NOS protein levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic administration of nicotine increases NO metabolites in all brain regions examined in both male and female rat.
the chronic nicotine administration increased the NO levels in all brain regions studied, but the cellular sources for this rise are probably not neurons.

chronic nicotine exposure in rats induces NO production and this increase in the NO levels in brain is not due to an increase in the number of neurons that express NOS, but rather to an increase in other sources of NO.
The main takeaway from our work is that

chronic nicotine administration in the rat brain results in an increase in NO metabolite levels, but not in the number of NO‐producing neurons, suggesting that the increase in NO levels may not be due to the activation of neuronal NO synthase.
chronic administration of nicotine does increase the levels of nitric oxide (as measured by NO metabolites) in the brain.
chronic nicotine exposure increases nitrate/nitrites in brain areas, but the source of this NO is not the NOS‐expressing neurons.
